prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B048 as my preferred configuration, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The chair asked whether a three-name citation can be drafted that is accurate about who did what. I think it can, if it is bounded to the Z2 insulating state and the quantum spin Hall effect and not to topological insulators as a whole. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the idea that spin-orbit coupling can produce a time-reversal-protected insulating state with helical edge states; Molenkamp's group then produced the decisive experimental evidence, quantized edge conductance in HgTe wells. That is a prediction followed by an unambiguous measurement, confirmed over about two decades by transport, ARPES and microscopy in several material families. Observation of a quantized edge conductance is a cleaner experimental signature than anything on the shortlist except possibly the clock comparisons. As a microscopist I also value that the result is not tied to one instrument: independent probes agree on the physics. I do not treat the number of supporters as evidence. I treat it as a reason to test my own reading, and after testing it I still find the science stronger than the alternatives.
statement.case_against: The attribution weakness is real and I will not minimise it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang identified the HgTe well as the platform and the inverted band structure with a critical thickness, which is what told Molenkamp where to look, and no three-name citation can include them alongside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp without dropping someone. The 3D topological insulator work and the first ARPES discoveries also sit outside. If a majority judged that the HgTe prediction is part of the core discovery and cannot be omitted, the configuration would be unsound as a single prize. There is also the overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases, which the committee must be ready to explain. I think the distinction holds (a time-reversal-invariant, symmetry-protected band insulator, not integer quantum Hall states or defect-driven transitions), but it needs to be stated plainly in the citation and not left to the reader.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B016 because it combines a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald) with a decisive experiment, has the broadest opening support, and he accepts that the pairing mechanism is open and that co-first authors Cao and Fatemi fall outside the three names.
responses.response: I accept the logic of prediction followed by experiment, which is the same logic I apply to B048, and I list B016 as my first alternative for that reason. Where I differ is on how settled the object is. For B048 the quantized edge channel and the Z2 classification have been stable for two decades, so a citation can name the phenomenon with no hedging. For B016 the citation has to be restricted to the flat bands and the existence of correlated and superconducting states, and the field is only about seven years past the experiments with the mechanism still contested; a prize committee that has said it rewards a discovery, not a promise, should be more cautious about that. I also note that the attribution problem in B016 is of the same kind as mine in B048, since the experimental team of Cao, Fatemi, Jarillo-Herrero is cut to one name. So I do not think B016 escapes the credit objection that Pearce is rightly pressing on others, and if the committee prefers it I would not oppose it strongly.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B049 first, arguing that magic-wavelength trapping is a new principle and not a refinement, with the cleanest two-name credit, and she worries about the 2016 overlap and the BHZ credit gap for B048.
responses.response: I agree that B049 has the cleanest credit on the list and I keep it as an alternative. I find the magic-wavelength idea more than engineering, and I withdraw the suggestion in my first statement that its impact is too narrow, because the redefinition of the second and the geodesy applications are broad in practice. My remaining hesitation is the one Lindroth herself raises, that the priority among early lattice-clock proposers and the JILA and Tokyo teams is not fully documented in what we have, and the comb and ion-control prizes already cover much of the toolkit. On the overlap she presses on B048, I take it as a real cost, but 2016 honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases, and this is a different class of matter: a band insulator whose protection comes from time reversal and spin-orbit coupling and was predicted before any material was known. That separation I can state in a citation. The BHZ gap, I agree, is the harder point.

responses.point: Kroll, as an atomic physicist, prefers B049 and sees B020 and B048 as his next choices, noting a JILA connection to Ye's laboratory.
responses.response: Kroll's disclosure matters here, because the case for B049 rests partly on priority statements that I cannot check from the record, and I would weigh the committee's judgement of that evidence over any single member's recollection, including his. I do not read the disclosure as disqualifying, and he lists B048 second, which suggests he regards the two as comparable in maturity. The point on which I would press him is his question of novelty: if the committee is asked to distinguish the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, someone who prefers B049 must say what the new physical principle is, and I think he can, but it is a narrower argument than the one available for B048.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B038 to B048 for the committee-wide support but warns that the credit line through the BHZ and 3D work is hard to draw, and that overlap with the 2016 prize and with B016 is a possible objection.
responses.response: I respect that Johansson placed his own colleagues' judgement above his proximity to circuit QED, and I do the same in not pressing B038, where I would also have to settle which of four names to drop. His question about the credit line is the real test for my choice. My answer is that the line is drawn at the Z2 state and its first observation, and it is a defensible place to draw it: Kane-Mele supply the concept and Molenkamp the experiment, and the BHZ proposal is cited in the discussion as the step that made the HgTe experiment possible. If he or others find that line unprincipled, I would want to hear the alternative wording in the final round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a citation limited to the Z2 state and its first observation is adequate when Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the three names; this is the single point that could move me to B016.
Whether the 2016 prize is read as covering the topological theme closely enough to count against a second award in the area, or whether time-reversal-invariant insulators are a distinct achievement.
Whether roughly seven years of confirmation for twisted bilayer graphene is enough, given the unsettled pairing mechanism, compared with two decades for B048 and B049.
How reliable the priority claims for early lattice clocks are, since they come from members' recollection and not from the supplied record.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name in B048, B016 or B049 is documented in my profile. I note again that Göran Johansson is at Chalmers, which is a colleague connection and not related to any candidate. My microscopy work on oxide interfaces and nanostructures is a general field overlap with moire and topological materials, not a personal or collaborative tie to any named person. I have no wish to recuse myself from any part of the vote, and I have noted Kroll's and Johansson's disclosures when weighing their statements.
